We will use AD and BC (abbreviations for Anno Domini and Before Christ )

(NOT the less-frequently used alternatives CE / Common Era and BCE / Before the Common Era)

Proper notation involves placing AD before the year, while BC comes after - no spaces between letters and numbers. 

(Example: AD2015 310BC etc - NOT 2015AD or 2015 AD or BC310 BC 310 etc.)

See more in < dynasties > and < BC > entries in Tansa 

AD is an abbreviation for Anno Domini, which translates as “in the year of the Lord” and denotes the years following Jesus Christ’s birth.  (it does not mean “after death”) 

BC means Before Christ and refers to the years leading up to Christ’s birth, counting backwards to an undefined point.

Use anti with a hyphen when it means opposed to, against or unlike the conventional form, and where the second part of the compound begins with an i: 

 anti-aircraft, anti-Aids, anti-Christ, anti-communist, anti-government, anti-hero, anti-inflammatory, anti-nuclear, anti-racism, anti-static, anti-tank 

 There is no hyphen when anti means preventing, relieving or the opposite of: 

 antibacterial, anticlimax, anticoagulant, antidepressant, antioxidant, antipruritic ,  antiretroviral, antitrust, antisocial 

 A compound noun which would not normally take a hyphen needs one if it is preceded by anti: 

 anti-money-laundering measures, anti-race-hate law, anti-bird-flu measures

Many of Hong Kong's islands have English names. Several are still referred to only by their English names, but others are increasingly known by their Chinese names. The Cantonese word chau means island, but frequently this is dropped.

Belt and Road Initiative (not BRI / lower-case "belt and road" unless full term used "Belt and Road Initiative" - no quote marks needed )

The central government's trade initiative to link economies into a China-centred trading network is now called the Belt and Road Initiative after a quiet rebranding. Do not use the previous "One Belt, One Road" name. We have stopped putting it in quote marks on first reference. 

Note the style: with caps when using the formal name of the initiative itself on first reference only. There is no need for caps when using the words belt and road in other ways, for example "companies that will benefit from the belt and road strategy", or in headlines. Try and avoid using the full title in headlines.

The initiative needs to be defined on first reference: China's plan to grow global trade, or similar. On subsequent references it can be simply referred to as the belt and road plan/strategy, or just the trade strategy or similar, no quote marks needed. Do not use the acronyms BRI or OBOR unless they are in a quote, when it should be followed by an explanation (eg xxx, she said, referring to the belt and road plan).  Also do not use belt and road as a noun, for example "countries along the belt and road". Belt and road is a strategy, not a physical entity, and covers many countries and trade routes. Say "countries that have signed up to the belt and road plan" or "countries along the belt and road plan's trade routes" or something similar.   

Finally, do not refer to this plan as "China's Marshall Plan", a term some western media have used. The Marshall Plan was aimed at rescuing economies shattered by war, the belt and road plan is a trade growth strategy.

Occupy Central

This civil-disobedience movement for universal suffrage was founded by academics Benny Tai Yiu-ting, an associate professor of law at the University of Hong Kong (note: he is NOT Dr Benny Tai Yiu-ting); the Reverend Chu Yiu-ming; and Dr Chan Kin-man, associate professor of sociology at Chinese University.  It planned to rally protesters to blockade Central district if the Hong Kong government did not come up with a satisfactory plan to implement universal suffrage for the election of the chief executive in 2017. The blockade was originally supposed to occur in summer 2014 but was actually declared on September 28, 2014, in Admiralty after students led by the Federation of Students occupied an area outside government headquarters in Admiralty known as Civic Square. Following the use of tear gas later that day, occupations spread to Nathan Road, Mong Kok, and to Yee Wo Street, Causeway Bay.  Injunctions to clear the Mong Kok protest and part of the Admiralty protest site were enforced in early December. The rest of the Admiralty site was then cleared and the final occupation zone, in Causeway Bay, was cleared on December 15, 2014, after which the chief executive, Leung Chun-ying, declared Occupy Central to be over. Police announced more than 900 arrests during the protests.  Because the protesters never in fact occupied Central, the movement is widely referred to simply as the Occupy movement. Post reports may also refer to it as such (note: Occupy movement, not Occupy Movement). See also: "umbrella movement".   Before Occupy Central began, supporters were asked, in July 2013, to take an oath to practise non-violence; it then held "deliberation days" in which supporters held discussions in schools and voted on their preferred proposals for universal suffrage; in spring 2014, a citywide ballot on the preferred proposals was held.

 We will not use the term “riot” for violent protests, or “rioters” for those taking part, because of complications with the legal implications of the word in Hong Kong courts.

Rivers  change name when they cross China's border, and in some cases within China. When referring to the name of a Chinese section of a river, add its other name in brackets the first time you refer to it.    So: the Yarlung Tsangpo (Brahmaputra)   the Nu (Salween) River  the Lancang (Mekong) River  the Tongtian He (Yangtze)  the Jinsha (Yangtze) River  the Tuotuo (Yangtze) River  the Heilong (Amur) River  the Hong or Yuan River (Red River)  the Xiangquan He (Sutlej)    In the case of the three upper sections of the Yangtze, use "Yangtze" in headlines    Some reports have come through to subeditors calling the Tuotuo, Tongtian or Jinsha tributaries or headstreams of the Yangtze. This is wrong - they are the names of different sections of the main stream of the river    The Yangtze River is, at 6,300km, the world's third-longest. Reports about the river as a whole should refer to "the Yangtze" (though Chinese people call the entire waterway the Chang Jiang, or Chang River; Chinese only call its lower reaches Yangtze)    The Chinese word for river is jiang or he. So stories should either use the Chinese or the English (and preferably the latter). The Nu River, not the Nujiang River. The Huai River, not the Huaihe River, The Tongtian River, not the Tongtian He River. And so on (see CHINESE GEOGRAPHICAL NAMES)

Hong Kong place names

In line with the government's Survey and Mapping Office, Hong Kong place names when rendered in English divide into two or three words according to how many characters their Chinese names contain. There are only three exceptions: Lamma Island, Lantau Island and Fanling. But note that, while Pok Fu Lam is three characters, we write Pokfulam Road (other roads which remain one word include Peiho St, Shunning Rd, Wuhu St); also note that in Sha Tin, we have Shatin Hospital    So please note that the following place names are, with effect from Sep 12 2006, written like this: Sha Tau Kok (not Shataukok) Hung Hom (not Hunghom), Lo Wu (not Lowu), Mong Kok (not Mongkok) Pok Fu Lam (not Pokfulam), Sha Lo Tung (not Shalotung), Sham Shui Po (not Shamshuipo), Shek Kip Mei (not Shekkipmei). Note that there is a Tai Koo station on the MTR, but the nearby office complex is called Taikoo Place and adjoins Taikoo Shing     Note also that the Survey and Mapping Office writes Shek Kong (not Sek Kong) for the area near Yuen Long housing a military base, so Post style changes accordingly    Please also take note that several islands and other coastal features with English names are more often referred to these days by their Chinese name. Where this is the case, the English name should be stated in brackets after the first mention of the Chinese name eg. Kat O (Crooked Island), Yan Chau Tong (Double Haven). South Korean place names

South Korea changed its system for Romanisation of place names in 2000. its main effect was to soften hard consonants (some Ps become Bs, Ch becomes J, T beomes D, K becomes G etc) and o becomes eo (so Kyongju is now written Gyeongju and Inchon becomes Incheon)    The United Nations has now adopted South Korea's revised Romanisation system. Therefore the Post will do so too.    Here are the new (and old) names for some places that crop up often in our reports (see end of this entry for a link to UN website with list of more South Korean place names):     Daegu not Taegu  Busan not Pusan  Gwangju not Kwangju  Jeju not Cheju  Dokdo not Tokdo  Incheon not Inchon    North Korea has not changed its system of Romanisation: Taepodong, not Daepodong, for North Korea's ballistic missile    Koreans do not use the name Sea of Japan for the sea separating Japan from the Korean peninsula. So Post reports should refer to this sea as: "the Sea of Japan, or East Sea"     Here is a link to a UN website listing the spellings of more places in South Korea   https://cag.scmp.com/CitrixWebProxy/aHR0cDovL3Vuc3RhdHMudW4ub3Jn/unsd/geoinfo/geonames/

Intersex people are people with both male and female biological sex characteristics. They should not automatically be referred to as transgender, although some may consider themselves such. 

 Don't write about an intersex person being "born a man" or "really being a man" or woman, or male or female, even if they discover they have another gender's sex characteristics later in life. 

 Refer to the person using the gender and pronouns they prefer (eg. “she/her”). In line with the government's Survey and Mapping Office, Hong Kong place names when rendered in English divide into two or three words according to how many characters their Chinese names contain. There are only three exceptions: Lamma Island, Lantau Island and Fanling. But note that, while Pok Fu Lam is three characters, we write Pokfulam Road (other roads which remain one word include Peiho St, Shunning Rd, Wuhu St); also note that in Sha Tin, we have Shatin Hospital    So please note that the following place names are, with effect from Sep 12 2006, written like this: Sha Tau Kok (not Shataukok) Hung Hom (not Hunghom), Lo Wu (not Lowu), Mong Kok (not Mongkok) Pok Fu Lam (not Pokfulam), Sha Lo Tung (not Shalotung), Sham Shui Po (not Shamshuipo), Shek Kip Mei (not Shekkipmei). Note that there is a Tai Koo station on the MTR, but the nearby office complex is called Taikoo Place and adjoins Taikoo Shing     Note also that the Survey and Mapping Office writes Shek Kong (not Sek Kong) for the area near Yuen Long housing a military base, so Post style changes accordingly    Please also take note that several islands and other coastal features with English names are more often referred to these days by their Chinese name. Where this is the case, the English name should be stated in brackets after the first mention of the Chinese name eg. Kat O (Crooked Island), Yan Chau Tong (Double Haven). See entries under Islands and Harbours and bays in the HK Place Names section of the Style Guide

Islands Many of Hong Kong's islands have English names. Several are still referred to only by their English names, but others are increasingly known by their Chinese names. The Cantonese word chau means island, but frequently this is dropped.

When we use an island's Chinese name, the English name should appear in brackets after it on first mention, as follows: Kat O (Crooked Island) Kiu Tsui Chau(Sharp Island) Pak Sha Chau in North District (Round Island) Leung Shuen Wan (High Island - but we still write High Island Reservoir) Wong Wan Chau (Double Island) Chek Chau (Port Island)

Some English names have dropped out of use: No one says Robinson Island any more, but Ap Chau; likewise, Pak Sha Chau in Sai Kung is never called White Sand Island; and Yeung Chau in Tolo Harbour is not referred to as Sheep Island

Equally, there are some islands whose English names are used, but rarely or hardly ever their Chinese names: Beaufort Island (not Lo Chau) Bluff Island (not Sha Tong Hau) Crescent Island (not Ngo Mei Chau) Town Island (not Fo Tau Fan Shau) Shelter Island (not Ngau Mei Shan) Basalt Island (not Fo Shek Chau) Sunshine Island

Most islands had never had English names eg. Cheung Chau, Peng Chau, Ping Chau, Po Toi

 How to calculate percentage increase, decrease or difference

1. Problem: You need to calculate per cent % increase from 2 to 10  2. First Step: find the difference between two numbers, in this case, it's 10 - 2 = 8  3. Second: Take the difference, 8, and divide by the original number: 8/2 = 4 4. Lastly, multiply the number above by 100: 4*100 = 400%  NB: when the mortgage rate jumps to 10 per cent from 8 per cent, it goes up 2 percentage points, not 2 per cent. When it jumps to 8.25 per cent from 8 per cent, it goes up either 25 basis points or a quarter of a percentage point. To write that it went up 0.25 of a percentage point is ugly.  When property prices soar to $6,000 a square foot from $2,000, they increase 200 per cent. But when prices fall to $2,000 from $6,000, we can't say they decline 200 per cent. they drop only 66.6 per cent. If something falls by 100 per cent, it drops to zero. Nothing can ever fall by more than 100 per cent - it is a logical impossibility.   Taking the above example, to find the size of a drop in percentage terms you need to perform the following calculation: 6,000 minus 2,000 divided by 6,000, then multiply the result by 100.   The same applies to phrases like a twofold fall, a tenfold drop - they are nonsense. If you see the phrase tenfold fall, it means something is only one tenth as big as it used to be; in other words, it has shrunk or fallen by 90 per cent. A twofold fall means something has fallen by 50 per cent. And so on.  Per cent means 'one part in every hundred". Figures should only be expressed as per cent in stories where the base figure is 100 or more, or the number of people surveyed IS PRETTY CLOSE TO OR exceeds 100. In stories which fail this test, we should simply cite the figures involved eg 45 of 74 respondents, 16 of 29 asked, 17 of the 41 questioned. After all, if murders go up from one to three, you could write that they have risen 200 per cent. It's an extreme example, but not that far away from what some reporters have written!

Hong Kong place names

In line with the government's Survey and Mapping Office, Hong Kong place names when rendered in English divide into two or three words according to how many characters their Chinese names contain. There are only three exceptions: Lamma Island, Lantau Island and Fanling. But note that, while Pok Fu Lam is three characters, we write Pokfulam Road (other roads which remain one word include Peiho St, Shunning Rd, Wuhu St); also note that in Sha Tin, we have Shatin Hospital    So please note that the following place names are, with effect from Sep 12 2006, written like this: Sha Tau Kok (not Shataukok) Hung Hom (not Hunghom), Lo Wu (not Lowu), Mong Kok (not Mongkok) Pok Fu Lam (not Pokfulam), Sha Lo Tung (not Shalotung), Sham Shui Po (not Shamshuipo), Shek Kip Mei (not Shekkipmei). Note that there is a Tai Koo station on the MTR, but the nearby office complex is called Taikoo Place and adjoins Taikoo Shing     Note also that the Survey and Mapping Office writes Shek Kong (not Sek Kong) for the area near Yuen Long housing a military base, so Post style changes accordingly    Please also take note that several islands and other coastal features with English names are more often referred to these days by their Chinese name. Where this is the case, the English name should be stated in brackets after the first mention of the Chinese name eg. Kat O (Crooked Island), Yan Chau Tong (Double Haven). Islands Many of Hong Kong's islands have English names. Several are still referred to only by their English names, but others are increasingly known by their Chinese names. The Cantonese word chau means island, but frequently this is dropped.

When we use an island's Chinese name, the English name should appear in brackets after it on first mention, as follows: Kat O (Crooked Island) Kiu Tsui Chau(Sharp Island) Pak Sha Chau in North District (Round Island) Leung Shuen Wan (High Island - but we still write High Island Reservoir) Wong Wan Chau (Double Island) Chek Chau (Port Island)

Some English names have dropped out of use: No one says Robinson Island any more, but Ap Chau; likewise, Pak Sha Chau in Sai Kung is never called White Sand Island; and Yeung Chau in Tolo Harbour is not referred to as Sheep Island

Equally, there are some islands whose English names are used, but rarely or hardly ever their Chinese names: Beaufort Island (not Lo Chau) Bluff Island (not Sha Tong Hau) Crescent Island (not Ngo Mei Chau) Town Island (not Fo Tau Fan Shau) Shelter Island (not Ngau Mei Shan) Basalt Island (not Fo Shek Chau) Sunshine Island

Most islands had never had English names eg. Cheung Chau, Peng Chau, Ping Chau, Po Toi

Hong Kong place names

In line with the government's Survey and Mapping Office, Hong Kong place names when rendered in English divide into two or three words according to how many characters their Chinese names contain. There are only three exceptions: Lamma Island, Lantau Island and Fanling. But note that, while Pok Fu Lam is three characters, we write Pokfulam Road (other roads which remain one word include Peiho St, Shunning Rd, Wuhu St); also note that in Sha Tin, we have Shatin Hospital    So please note that the following place names are, with effect from Sep 12 2006, written like this: Sha Tau Kok (not Shataukok) Hung Hom (not Hunghom), Lo Wu (not Lowu), Mong Kok (not Mongkok) Pok Fu Lam (not Pokfulam), Sha Lo Tung (not Shalotung), Sham Shui Po (not Shamshuipo), Shek Kip Mei (not Shekkipmei). Note that there is a Tai Koo station on the MTR, but the nearby office complex is called Taikoo Place and adjoins Taikoo Shing     Note also that the Survey and Mapping Office writes Shek Kong (not Sek Kong) for the area near Yuen Long housing a military base, so Post style changes accordingly    Please also take note that several islands and other coastal features with English names are more often referred to these days by their Chinese name. Where this is the case, the English name should be stated in brackets after the first mention of the Chinese name eg. Kat O (Crooked Island), Yan Chau Tong (Double Haven). Rivers   change name when they cross China's border, and in some cases within China. When referring to the name of a Chinese section of a river, add its other name in brackets the first time you refer to it.    So: the Yarlung Tsangpo (Brahmaputra)   the Nu (Salween) River  the Lancang (Mekong) River  the Tongtian He (Yangtze)  the Jinsha (Yangtze) River  the Tuotuo (Yangtze) River  the Heilong (Amur) River  the Hong or Yuan River (Red River)  the Xiangquan He (Sutlej)    In the case of the three upper sections of the Yangtze, use "Yangtze" in headlines    Some reports have come through to subeditors calling the Tuotuo, Tongtian or Jinsha tributaries or headstreams of the Yangtze. This is wrong - they are the names of different sections of the main stream of the river    The Yangtze River is, at 6,300km, the world's third-longest. Reports about the river as a whole should refer to "the Yangtze" (though Chinese people call the entire waterway the Chang Jiang, or Chang River; Chinese only call its lower reaches Yangtze)    The Chinese word for river is jiang or he. So stories should either use the Chinese or the English (and preferably the latter). The Nu River, not the Nujiang River. The Huai River, not the Huaihe River, The Tongtian River, not the Tongtian He River. And so on (see CHINESE GEOGRAPHICAL NAMES)

A transgender person is someone who identifies their gender as being different from the sex they were assigned at birth. Someone born with male sexual organs at birth but who now identifies as a woman is a trans woman, and someone born with female sexual organs at birth but who now identifies as a man is a trans man. Use the subject's own declared identity; the degree of their transition (social, hormonal, surgical) is irrelevant. 

 Always use the pronouns that the subject uses - "he/him", "she/her", "they/them" etc. Confirm their preferences with them if you can. In the case of someone who uses pronouns other than he/him and she/her, on first usage, introduce them along the lines of "Xxxx, who uses they/them pronouns".  Don't use scare quotes around non-traditional pronouns. 

 Similarly, do not refer to a trans woman as "having been born a man", or "really being a man" etc (and vice versa for trans men) unless they specifically use this language themselves - and then, for absolute clarity, only quote them directly. 

 Note that transgender is one word but trans man, trans woman and trans person are two words each, with spaces.  

 Always write < a transgender person > / < trans person > or < a person who identifies as transgender > etc (NOT < a transgender > or < transgenders >. 

For people who identify as other genders than man or woman, note spelling: non-binary (not nonbinary or non binary), genderfluid (not gender-fluid or gender fluid), genderqueer (not gender-queer or gender queer).

Do not confuse this loose grouping with the militant East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM) since they have the same initials. If you need to abbreviate East Turkestan Independence Movement, write "the independence movement". Islands Many of Hong Kong's islands have English names. Several are still referred to only by their English names, but others are increasingly known by their Chinese names. The Cantonese word chau means island, but frequently this is dropped.

When we use an island's Chinese name, the English name should appear in brackets after it on first mention, as follows: Kat O (Crooked Island) Kiu Tsui Chau(Sharp Island) Pak Sha Chau in North District (Round Island) Leung Shuen Wan (High Island - but we still write High Island Reservoir) Wong Wan Chau (Double Island) Chek Chau (Port Island)

Some English names have dropped out of use: No one says Robinson Island any more, but Ap Chau; likewise, Pak Sha Chau in Sai Kung is never called White Sand Island; and Yeung Chau in Tolo Harbour is not referred to as Sheep Island

Equally, there are some islands whose English names are used, but rarely or hardly ever their Chinese names: Beaufort Island (not Lo Chau) Bluff Island (not Sha Tong Hau) Crescent Island (not Ngo Mei Chau) Town Island (not Fo Tau Fan Shau) Shelter Island (not Ngau Mei Shan) Basalt Island (not Fo Shek Chau) Sunshine Island
